title: Know what good service should look like on the day
intro: A useful quality conversation is specific about the experience you have booked. It covers the agreed menu, service timing, staffing and the way concerns can be raised. This page explains how to make those expectations visible before an occasion and how to communicate if something needs attention. Any formal remedy or guarantee depends on the terms attached to your booking; the practical guidance here helps you assess the service and give the team information they can act on promptly.

sections.title: Use the agreed proposal as your reference
paragraphs: Keep the confirmed menu, guest count and included roles together so there is a clear picture of what should happen. If your plans change, request an updated confirmation rather than relying on a series of separate messages.

During service, raise a concern with the designated contact as soon as it is practical. Explain the issue and what would help, whether that is a timing adjustment, clarification about a dish or attention to an agreed task. Early, factual communication gives the team the best opportunity to assess the situation and respond within the scope of the booking.

sections.title: Confirm the practical details before the date is secured
paragraphs: A promising menu is only one part of a booking. Before confirming, review the date, address, guest count, arrival time, service hours and included roles. Make sure the dietary brief and any essential equipment requirements are reflected in the proposal rather than left in separate messages that can be overlooked.

Read the payment schedule and the terms that apply to your particular service. A recurring household plan and a one-off event may have different arrangements for changes, cancellation and outstanding balances. Use the terms attached to your booking rather than assuming a policy from another service or an earlier quotation automatically applies.

Keep one agreed version of the menu and scope. If you change the number of guests, request a new dish or move the meal time, ask for confirmation of any effect on staffing, availability and price. This creates a clear reference for you and the team and helps the chef prepare for the service you actually expect.

sections.title: Give every person in the service a clear role
paragraphs: Cooking, carrying plates, pouring drinks and clearing a table are different jobs. For a quiet household visit, you may need only a chef. For an occasion with several courses or guests arriving together, an assistant or service professional can help the kitchen and dining area run at the right pace. Staffing should follow the work, rather than a fixed assumption based only on headcount.

Discuss who will greet guests, replenish water, serve each course and clear used plates. If the chef is expected to do all of those tasks while cooking, the menu and timing need to allow for it. Extra support can be especially useful when the kitchen is far from the dining table or the meal involves several dietary variations.

Your proposal should identify the included roles and service hours. Additional hospitality, equipment and event coordination should be agreed as part of the scope. That clarity lets everyone focus on their responsibilities and gives you a more relaxed experience as host.

sections.title: Keep dietary variations manageable and well briefed
paragraphs: When guests have different requirements, a clear list is more useful than a series of last-minute messages. Record the requirement, how many people it applies to and whether it is a preference or an essential restriction. Where an allergy is involved, disclose it directly so the team can assess ingredients and kitchen conditions before accepting the request.

The menu can sometimes share a common foundation with a few carefully planned variations. Serving a sauce separately or choosing a side that suits several guests may make the experience simpler. In other cases, a distinct alternative dish is the better choice. The chef should recommend what is workable rather than assuming every recipe can be adapted successfully.

For plated service, agree how the correct dish will reach the correct guest. A seating plan or discreet identification method can help. Update the team if the guest list changes, and make sure the final menu reflects the confirmed requirements. Good preparation makes inclusive hosting feel natural at the table.

sections.title: End the visit with a clear kitchen handover
paragraphs: Before the chef leaves, make sure you understand what has been prepared and how it is intended to be used. Identify the meal for immediate service, the portions prepared for later and any dish that still needs a finishing step. Written labels or agreed notes can be useful when another family member will be serving the food.

Check the practical points that matter to your home: where containers have been placed, which serving items are in use and whether ingredients remain for the next visit. The agreed cleanup scope should also be clear, including the work surfaces and equipment used during cooking. A good handover reduces the need to search for information after the service has ended.

For a recurring plan, note anything that needs replenishing or changing before the next appointment. For a one-off dinner, confirm how any hired items or additional equipment will be collected. The final few minutes should leave you with a usable kitchen and a clear understanding of the food and arrangements.

sections.title: Make feedback specific enough to act on
paragraphs: The easiest way to improve an ongoing service is to describe the result you want. Instead of saying a meal was not right, explain whether it was too rich, too spicy, too large or served later than expected. A specific observation gives the chef a useful direction for the next menu and makes it easier to check whether the adjustment worked.

Tell us what you enjoyed as well. A dish you would happily eat again, a helpful way of organising the fridge or a cooking day that fitted your schedule can become part of the regular plan. Consistency is built from these details, not simply from repeating a menu without checking how it is being used.

For a service concern, contact myCHEF promptly with the relevant facts. The next step may be a menu change, a clearer brief, a revised schedule or discussion of a different available match. Any remedy depends on the circumstances and the booking terms; the starting point is a clear conversation.

sections.title: Judge the service by the difference it makes at home
paragraphs: The value of a private chef is not measured only by the number of dishes prepared. Consider whether the meals are being enjoyed, whether the timing works and whether the arrangement reduces the decisions you need to make each day. A reliable favourite served when you need it can be more useful than an ambitious menu that does not fit your routine.

Review the service against the priorities in your original brief. Are the portions right? Is shopping clear? Do you understand what is ready for later? Are the booked hours being used for the tasks you care about most? These questions help you identify a practical adjustment before deciding that the whole arrangement needs to change.

For an occasion, think about your experience as host as well as the food. Clear coordination, suitable staffing and a manageable service format can give you more time with guests. The best proposal is the one that connects its price and scope to the experience you actually want.

cta.body: Share your date or preferred cooking schedule, Dubai location and the number of people you are planning for. Tell us what you would most like help with, and we will discuss a suitable menu and service arrangement before confirming the details in writing.
